**Sean Thomas Casey** (born July 2, 1974),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-1) nicknamed "**the Mayor**", is an American former professional [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball")[first baseman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_baseman "First baseman"), [coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coach_(baseball) "Coach (baseball)") and media personality. During his [Major League Baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball "Major League Baseball") (MLB) career, Casey played for the [Cleveland Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Indians "Cleveland Indians"), [Cincinnati Reds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati_Reds "Cincinnati Reds"), [Pittsburgh Pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Pirates "Pittsburgh Pirates"), [Detroit Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Tigers "Detroit Tigers"), and [Boston Red Sox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Red_Sox "Boston Red Sox"). Casey was selected to the [MLB All-Star Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball_All-Star_Game "Major League Baseball All-Star Game") three times during his career.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-3) He was the hitting coach for the [New York Yankees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Yankees "New York Yankees") in 2023. After retiring from professional baseball, Casey transitioned into broadcasting and has been a prominent broadcaster and commentator for [MLB Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MLB_Network "MLB Network")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:0-4) since 2009, a role he still holds today. In addition to his broadcasting work, Casey is the host of the popular “The Mayor’s Office with Sean Casey” podcast, where he shares engaging conversations with athletes, entertainers, and industry leaders.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Casey was born in [Willingboro, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willingboro,_New_Jersey "Willingboro, New Jersey"), the son of Joan and Jim Casey. He and his family moved to [Upper St. Clair Township, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_St._Clair_Township,_Pennsylvania "Upper St. Clair Township, Pennsylvania"), when he was a child. He graduated from [Upper St. Clair High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_St._Clair_High_School "Upper St. Clair High School") in Upper St. Clair,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-5) and the [University of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Richmond "University of Richmond") in [Richmond, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond,_Virginia "Richmond, Virginia"), where he played [college baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_baseball "College baseball") for the [Richmond Spiders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond_Spiders_baseball "Richmond Spiders baseball").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-reflection-6)

As a freshman for the Spiders in 1993, Casey had a .386 [batting average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batting_average_(baseball) "Batting average (baseball)"), a .447 [on-base percentage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-base_percentage "On-base percentage") (OBP), and a .526 SLG, with two home runs. He was named a freshman [All-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-American "All-American")[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-7) and second team All-[Colonial Athletic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_Athletic_Association "Colonial Athletic Association") (CAA).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-CAA-8)

As a sophomore in 1994, Casey batted .371 with a .656 SLG, 13 home runs, and 57 [runs batted in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runs_batted_in "Runs batted in") (RBIs). He was named first team All-CAA.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-CAA-8) Following his sophomore season at Richmond, Casey played [collegiate summer baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collegiate_summer_baseball "Collegiate summer baseball") for the [Brewster Whitecaps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brewster_Whitecaps "Brewster Whitecaps") of the [Cape Cod Baseball League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Baseball_League "Cape Cod Baseball League") (CCBL), where he batted .338 with one home run and 30 RBIs, and was named a league all-star.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-9) In 2003, he was inducted into the [CCBL Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Baseball_League#Hall_of_Fame_and_Museum "Cape Cod Baseball League").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-10)

In the 1995 season as a junior, Casey hit for a .461 batting average to lead all [Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_I_(NCAA) "Division I (NCAA)") players.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:1-11) Casey was again named first team All-CAA and won the CAA Player of the Year.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-CAA-8) He was also named a Second Team All-American and ECAC Player of the Year while becoming the first player to ever win the CAA Triple Crown.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:2-12) He graduated from Richmond and was a member of [Sigma Phi Epsilon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigma_Phi_Epsilon "Sigma Phi Epsilon") fraternity.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-reflection-6)

## Playing career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Playing career")]

### Cleveland Indians

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Cleveland Indians")]

The [Cleveland Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Indians "Cleveland Indians") chose Casey in the second round, with the 53rd overall selection, of the [1995 MLB draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_MLB_draft "1995 MLB draft").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-13) Casey began his professional career with the [Watertown Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watertown_Indians "Watertown Indians") of the [Class A-Short Season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_A-Short_Season "Class A-Short Season")[New York–Penn League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York%E2%80%93Penn_League "New York–Penn League"), where he batted .329 with two home runs. He was promoted to the [Kinston Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinston_Indians "Kinston Indians") of the [Class A-Advanced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_A-Advanced "Class A-Advanced")[Carolina League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolina_League "Carolina League") to begin the 1996 season. He hit .331 with twelve home runs for Kinston.

Casey started 1997 with the [Akron Aeros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akron_RubberDucks "Akron RubberDucks") of the [Class AA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_AA "Class AA")[Eastern League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_League_(1938%E2%80%932020) "Eastern League (1938–2020)"). On June 18, the Indians promoted Casey to the [Buffalo Bisons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Bisons "Buffalo Bisons") of the [Class AAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_AAA "Class AAA")[American Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Association_(20th_century) "American Association (20th century)") after batting .386 with 19 doubles, 10 home runs and 66 RBIs in 62 games with Akron. In 20 games with Buffalo, Casey hit five home runs and 18 RBIs. On September 12, Casey was promoted to the Cleveland Indians as a [September call-up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_call-ups "September call-ups"). He appeared in six games for the Indians, going 2-for-10 (.200) with two walks and one RBI. Casey won the Lou Boudreau Award as the Cleveland Indians' top minor-league position player, at the conclusion of the 1997 season.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-14)_[Baseball America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball\_America "Baseball America")_ named him the No.20 prospect in baseball before the 1998 season.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-15)

### Cincinnati Reds

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Cincinnati Reds")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Baseball_first_baseman_2004.jpg/250px-Baseball_first_baseman_2004.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Baseball_first_baseman_2004.jpg)

Casey with the [Cincinnati Reds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati_Reds "Cincinnati Reds") in 2004

On March 30, 1998, Casey was traded to the [Cincinnati Reds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati_Reds "Cincinnati Reds") for [Dave Burba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Burba "Dave Burba").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-16) On April 3, [1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Cincinnati_Reds_season "1998 Cincinnati Reds season"), Casey was hit in the eye with a ball thrown by teammate [Damian Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damian_Jackson_(baseball) "Damian Jackson (baseball)") during batting practice, resulting in an orbital fracture, and subsequent surgery.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-17) Casey's surgery took two surgeons, operating for four hours to fix his fracture.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-surgery-18) Just three weeks after the surgery, Casey began his rehab assignment with the [Indianapolis Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indianapolis_Indians "Indianapolis Indians"), and just a week after joining the Indians, he was recalled to the Reds.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-surgery-18) Casey struggled during his first season with the Reds, his average dipped to .133, and he was sent back to Indianapolis.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-19) On June 18, Casey was recalled to the Reds.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-20)

On May 19, [1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Cincinnati_Reds_season "1999 Cincinnati Reds season"), the Reds defeated the [Colorado Rockies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Colorado_Rockies_season "1999 Colorado Rockies season") in a 24−12 final, tied for the fourth-highest run-scoring output in MLB history. Casey hit two of the Reds' six home runs, and reached base seven times with four hits and three walks. He also scored five runs and [drove in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Run_batted_in "Run batted in") six.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-21) He was selected to the [All-Star Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Major_League_Baseball_All-Star_Game "1999 Major League Baseball All-Star Game") for the first time in 1999. Casey produced a breakout offensive season in 1999, batting .332 with 25 home runs, 99 RBIs, 42 [doubles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_(baseball) "Double (baseball)"), and 103 runs scored in 151 games. He was fourth in the National League in batting and doubles, and sixth in [singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(baseball) "Single (baseball)"). In 1999, he won the [Hutch Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hutch_Award "Hutch Award").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:3-22)

During his tenure in Cincinnati, and later in Pittsburgh and Detroit, Casey was regarded as approachable and friendly, and his nickname, "the Mayor", comes from his reputation for chatting casually with every runner who makes it to first base, and from his very public charity work. It was frequently expanded to "the Mayor of Riverfront" when the Reds played at [Riverfront Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverfront_Stadium "Riverfront Stadium"). On May 16, 2007, Casey was voted in 2007 as "the friendliest player in baseball" by fellow players in a Sports Illustrated poll.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:4-23) He garnered 46% of the vote with the second place vote being split between [Jim Thome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Thome "Jim Thome") and [Mike Sweeney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Sweeney "Mike Sweeney") with only 7% each. Casey was also regarded as among the slowest-running players in the game, grounding into 27 [double plays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_play "Double play") in the 2005 season. This tied him with [A. J. Pierzynski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._J._Pierzynski "A. J. Pierzynski") for the record of most grounding in double plays by a National League left-handed batter in a season.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-24)

### Pittsburgh Pirates

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Pittsburgh Pirates")]

On December 8, 2005, Casey was traded to his hometown [Pittsburgh Pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Pirates "Pittsburgh Pirates") for [left-handed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-handed "Left-handed") pitcher [Dave Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Williams_(2000s_pitcher) "Dave Williams (2000s pitcher)").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-25) On April 14, 2006, Casey left a game against the [Chicago Cubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Cubs "Chicago Cubs") after suffering two fractures of the [transverse process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transverse_process "Transverse process") in his lower left back. He was placed on the disabled list on April 15.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-26) After a rehab assignment with the [Altoona Curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altoona_Curve "Altoona Curve"),[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-27) Casey returned to the Pirates lineup. He played in 59 games for the Pirates during the 2006 season, batted .296 with three home runs and 29 RBIs.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Detroit Tigers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Detroit Tigers")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Sean_Casey.jpg/250px-Sean_Casey.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sean_Casey.jpg)

Casey with the [Detroit Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Tigers "Detroit Tigers") in 2007

On July 31, 2006, the Pirates traded Casey to the [Detroit Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Tigers "Detroit Tigers") for minor league pitcher [Brian Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Rogers_(baseball) "Brian Rogers (baseball)").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-28) During the [2006 American League Championship Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_American_League_Championship_Series "2006 American League Championship Series") against the [Oakland Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakland_Athletics "Oakland Athletics"), he partially tore his left calf muscle in Game 1.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-29) After coming back from his torn calf in Game 2 of the World Series, Casey became the hottest hitter for the Tigers, belting two home runs and batting .432 in five games. His .432 batting average was one of the best in Tigers' postseason history.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-30)

Casey has been active in [Big Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Brothers_Big_Sisters_of_America "Big Brothers Big Sisters of America") and [Make-A-Wish Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Make-A-Wish_Foundation "Make-A-Wish Foundation"), as well as the "Casey's Crew" program, where he provided free high-priced tickets to disadvantaged youth.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-31) Casey credits his [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians "Christians") upbringing in Pittsburgh's affluent [Upper St. Clair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_St._Clair_Township,_Pennsylvania "Upper St. Clair Township, Pennsylvania") suburb for his generosity.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-32)

After being told by [Dave Dombrowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Dombrowski "Dave Dombrowski") and [Jim Leyland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Leyland "Jim Leyland") that he would not be re-signed, Casey still praised [Mike Ilitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Ilitch "Mike Ilitch"), Dombrowski, and Jim Leyland for giving him the opportunity to come play for Detroit. Casey said "They let me know. I've had a great time with this team, the greatest year and a half of my career. It was great. But I understand the situation."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-33)

### Boston Red Sox

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Boston Red Sox")]

On February 5, 2008, the [Boston Red Sox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Red_Sox "Boston Red Sox") announced they had signed Casey to a one-year deal.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-34) On April 9, 2008, Red Sox third baseman [Mike Lowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Lowell "Mike Lowell") injured his thumb and was then placed on the DL, first baseman [Kevin Youkilis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Youkilis "Kevin Youkilis") was moved to third, and Casey stepped in as the starting first baseman[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-35) and exploded by making some good defensive plays and hitting .318 with five RBIs in his first seven games despite missing games in [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") due to a [stiff neck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neck_stiffness "Neck stiffness") he received during the 18-hour flight.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-36) He was on the disabled list from April 26 through May 12, and returned as a significant part-time player, finishing the regular season with a .773 OPS on 199 at-bats in 69 games.

Casey was suspended by the [MLB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MLB "MLB") for three games after his actions in the [Coco Crisp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coco_Crisp "Coco Crisp")–[James Shields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Shields_(pitcher) "James Shields (pitcher)") brawl.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-37)

## Post-playing career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Post-playing career")]

Casey announced his retirement on January 25, 2009, at the age of 34, having played 12 seasons of Major League Baseball. He accepted a position as a baseball analyst for [MLB Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MLB_Network "MLB Network").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-38) He appeared on _[MLB Tonight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MLB\_Tonight "MLB Tonight")_, the Spring Training series _30 Clubs in 30 Days_, the children-focused weekly interview and demonstration show _Play Ball_ and MLB Network's special event coverage throughout the year.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:0-4)

On July 3, 2009, Casey sat in for Red Sox [color commentator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_commentator "Color commentator")[Jerry Remy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Remy "Jerry Remy"), calling the first game for his old team. On January 14, 2011, the Reds announced that Casey would do [color commentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_commentator "Color commentator") for 15 telecasts on [Fox Sports Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Sports_Ohio "Fox Sports Ohio") during the 2011 season.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-39)

The [New York Yankees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Yankees "New York Yankees") hired Casey as their [hitting coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hitting_coach "Hitting coach") on July 10, 2023.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-40)

## Awards and accomplishments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Awards and accomplishments")]

*   [National League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_League_(baseball) "National League (baseball)")[All-Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball_All-Star_Game "Major League Baseball All-Star Game"), 1999, 2001, 2004
*   [Hutch Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hutch_Award "Hutch Award"), 1999 given to the player who personifies the spirit, courage and integrity of former manager Fred Hutchinson.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:3-22)
*   Inducted into the [University of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Richmond "University of Richmond"), Department of Athletics Hall of Fame[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:1-11) in 2003.

With [Conan O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan_O'Brien "Conan O'Brien"), Casey is a founder of Labels Are For Jars,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-41) an innovative anti-hunger organization based in [Lawrence, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence,_Massachusetts "Lawrence, Massachusetts").

In a May 16, 2007, _[Sports Illustrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated "Sports Illustrated")_ Player's Poll,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:4-23) Casey won the distinction of being considered the "friendliest player in baseball", after winning 46% of the votes. 464 MLB players participated in the survey. [Hal McCoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_McCoy "Hal McCoy"), a Cincinnati Reds beat writer for 35 years, has said, "There's no debate, and there never will be a debate. Sean Casey is the nicest guy in professional baseball. Ever."

On August 26, 2008, Casey was inducted into the Irish American Baseball Hall of Fame.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-42)

On January 29, 2009, Casey was inducted into the Kinston Professional Baseball Hall of Fame.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-43)

Casey was inducted to the [Cincinnati Reds Baseball Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati_Reds_Hall_of_Fame_and_Museum "Cincinnati Reds Hall of Fame and Museum") (along with [Dan Driessen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Driessen "Dan Driessen") and [John Reilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Reilly_(baseball) "John Reilly (baseball)")) on June 23, 2012.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:2-12)

In 2014, Casey was inducted into the [Virginia Sports Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Sports_Hall_of_Fame_and_Museum "Virginia Sports Hall of Fame and Museum").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-44)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Casey resides in Upper St. Clair Township, Pennsylvania, with his wife, Sarah. **Sean Thomas Casey** (born July 2, 1974),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-1) nicknamed "**the Mayor**", is an American former professional [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball")[first baseman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_baseman "First baseman"), [coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coach_(baseball) "Coach (baseball)") and media personality. During his [Major League Baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball "Major League Baseball") (MLB) career, Casey played for the [Cleveland Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Indians "Cleveland Indians"), [Cincinnati Reds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati_Reds "Cincinnati Reds"), [Pittsburgh Pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Pirates "Pittsburgh Pirates"), [Detroit Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Tigers "Detroit Tigers"), and [Boston Red Sox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Red_Sox "Boston Red Sox"). Casey was selected to the [MLB All-Star Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball_All-Star_Game "Major League Baseball All-Star Game") three times during his career.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-3) He was the hitting coach for the [New York Yankees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Yankees "New York Yankees") in 2023. After retiring from professional baseball, Casey transitioned into broadcasting and has been a prominent broadcaster and commentator for [MLB Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MLB_Network "MLB Network")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:0-4) since 2009, a role he still holds today. In addition to his broadcasting work, Casey is the host of the popular “The Mayor’s Office with Sean Casey” podcast, where he shares engaging conversations with athletes, entertainers, and industry leaders.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Casey was born in [Willingboro, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willingboro,_New_Jersey "Willingboro, New Jersey"), the son of Joan and Jim Casey. He and his family moved to [Upper St. Clair Township, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_St._Clair_Township,_Pennsylvania "Upper St. Clair Township, Pennsylvania"), when he was a child. He graduated from [Upper St. Clair High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_St._Clair_High_School "Upper St. Clair High School") in Upper St. Clair,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-5) and the [University of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Richmond "University of Richmond") in [Richmond, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond,_Virginia "Richmond, Virginia"), where he played [college baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_baseball "College baseball") for the [Richmond Spiders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richmond_Spiders_baseball "Richmond Spiders baseball").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-reflection-6)

As a freshman for the Spiders in 1993, Casey had a .386 [batting average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batting_average_(baseball) "Batting average (baseball)"), a .447 [on-base percentage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On-base_percentage "On-base percentage") (OBP), and a .526 SLG, with two home runs. He was named a freshman [All-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-American "All-American")[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-7) and second team All-[Colonial Athletic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_Athletic_Association "Colonial Athletic Association") (CAA).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-CAA-8)

As a sophomore in 1994, Casey batted .371 with a .656 SLG, 13 home runs, and 57 [runs batted in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runs_batted_in "Runs batted in") (RBIs). He was named first team All-CAA.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-CAA-8) Following his sophomore season at Richmond, Casey played [collegiate summer baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collegiate_summer_baseball "Collegiate summer baseball") for the [Brewster Whitecaps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brewster_Whitecaps "Brewster Whitecaps") of the [Cape Cod Baseball League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Baseball_League "Cape Cod Baseball League") (CCBL), where he batted .338 with one home run and 30 RBIs, and was named a league all-star.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-9) In 2003, he was inducted into the [CCBL Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Baseball_League#Hall_of_Fame_and_Museum "Cape Cod Baseball League").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-10)

In the 1995 season as a junior, Casey hit for a .461 batting average to lead all [Division I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_I_(NCAA) "Division I (NCAA)") players.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:1-11) Casey was again named first team All-CAA and won the CAA Player of the Year.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-CAA-8) He was also named a Second Team All-American and ECAC Player of the Year while becoming the first player to ever win the CAA Triple Crown.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:2-12) He graduated from Richmond and was a member of [Sigma Phi Epsilon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigma_Phi_Epsilon "Sigma Phi Epsilon") fraternity.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-reflection-6)

## Playing career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Playing career")]

### Cleveland Indians

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Cleveland Indians")]

The [Cleveland Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Indians "Cleveland Indians") chose Casey in the second round, with the 53rd overall selection, of the [1995 MLB draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_MLB_draft "1995 MLB draft").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-13) Casey began his professional career with the [Watertown Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watertown_Indians "Watertown Indians") of the [Class A-Short Season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_A-Short_Season "Class A-Short Season")[New York–Penn League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York%E2%80%93Penn_League "New York–Penn League"), where he batted .329 with two home runs. He was promoted to the [Kinston Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinston_Indians "Kinston Indians") of the [Class A-Advanced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_A-Advanced "Class A-Advanced")[Carolina League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolina_League "Carolina League") to begin the 1996 season. He hit .331 with twelve home runs for Kinston.

Casey started 1997 with the [Akron Aeros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akron_RubberDucks "Akron RubberDucks") of the [Class AA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_AA "Class AA")[Eastern League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_League_(1938%E2%80%932020) "Eastern League (1938–2020)"). On June 18, the Indians promoted Casey to the [Buffalo Bisons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo_Bisons "Buffalo Bisons") of the [Class AAA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_AAA "Class AAA")[American Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Association_(20th_century) "American Association (20th century)") after batting .386 with 19 doubles, 10 home runs and 66 RBIs in 62 games with Akron. In 20 games with Buffalo, Casey hit five home runs and 18 RBIs. On September 12, Casey was promoted to the Cleveland Indians as a [September call-up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_call-ups "September call-ups"). He appeared in six games for the Indians, going 2-for-10 (.200) with two walks and one RBI. Casey won the Lou Boudreau Award as the Cleveland Indians' top minor-league position player, at the conclusion of the 1997 season.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-14)_[Baseball America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball\_America "Baseball America")_ named him the No.20 prospect in baseball before the 1998 season.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-15)

### Cincinnati Reds

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Cincinnati Reds")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Baseball_first_baseman_2004.jpg/250px-Baseball_first_baseman_2004.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Baseball_first_baseman_2004.jpg)

Casey with the [Cincinnati Reds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati_Reds "Cincinnati Reds") in 2004

On March 30, 1998, Casey was traded to the [Cincinnati Reds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati_Reds "Cincinnati Reds") for [Dave Burba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Burba "Dave Burba").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-16) On April 3, [1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Cincinnati_Reds_season "1998 Cincinnati Reds season"), Casey was hit in the eye with a ball thrown by teammate [Damian Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damian_Jackson_(baseball) "Damian Jackson (baseball)") during batting practice, resulting in an orbital fracture, and subsequent surgery.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-17) Casey's surgery took two surgeons, operating for four hours to fix his fracture.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-surgery-18) Just three weeks after the surgery, Casey began his rehab assignment with the [Indianapolis Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indianapolis_Indians "Indianapolis Indians"), and just a week after joining the Indians, he was recalled to the Reds.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-surgery-18) Casey struggled during his first season with the Reds, his average dipped to .133, and he was sent back to Indianapolis.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-19) On June 18, Casey was recalled to the Reds.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-20)

On May 19, [1999](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Cincinnati_Reds_season "1999 Cincinnati Reds season"), the Reds defeated the [Colorado Rockies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Colorado_Rockies_season "1999 Colorado Rockies season") in a 24−12 final, tied for the fourth-highest run-scoring output in MLB history. Casey hit two of the Reds' six home runs, and reached base seven times with four hits and three walks. He also scored five runs and [drove in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Run_batted_in "Run batted in") six.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-21) He was selected to the [All-Star Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Major_League_Baseball_All-Star_Game "1999 Major League Baseball All-Star Game") for the first time in 1999. Casey produced a breakout offensive season in 1999, batting .332 with 25 home runs, 99 RBIs, 42 [doubles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_(baseball) "Double (baseball)"), and 103 runs scored in 151 games. He was fourth in the National League in batting and doubles, and sixth in [singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_(baseball) "Single (baseball)"). In 1999, he won the [Hutch Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hutch_Award "Hutch Award").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:3-22)

During his tenure in Cincinnati, and later in Pittsburgh and Detroit, Casey was regarded as approachable and friendly, and his nickname, "the Mayor", comes from his reputation for chatting casually with every runner who makes it to first base, and from his very public charity work. It was frequently expanded to "the Mayor of Riverfront" when the Reds played at [Riverfront Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverfront_Stadium "Riverfront Stadium"). On May 16, 2007, Casey was voted in 2007 as "the friendliest player in baseball" by fellow players in a Sports Illustrated poll.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:4-23) He garnered 46% of the vote with the second place vote being split between [Jim Thome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Thome "Jim Thome") and [Mike Sweeney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Sweeney "Mike Sweeney") with only 7% each. Casey was also regarded as among the slowest-running players in the game, grounding into 27 [double plays](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_play "Double play") in the 2005 season. This tied him with [A. J. Pierzynski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._J._Pierzynski "A. J. Pierzynski") for the record of most grounding in double plays by a National League left-handed batter in a season.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-24)

### Pittsburgh Pirates

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Pittsburgh Pirates")]

On December 8, 2005, Casey was traded to his hometown [Pittsburgh Pirates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh_Pirates "Pittsburgh Pirates") for [left-handed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-handed "Left-handed") pitcher [Dave Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Williams_(2000s_pitcher) "Dave Williams (2000s pitcher)").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-25) On April 14, 2006, Casey left a game against the [Chicago Cubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Cubs "Chicago Cubs") after suffering two fractures of the [transverse process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transverse_process "Transverse process") in his lower left back. He was placed on the disabled list on April 15.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-26) After a rehab assignment with the [Altoona Curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altoona_Curve "Altoona Curve"),[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-27) Casey returned to the Pirates lineup. He played in 59 games for the Pirates during the 2006 season, batted .296 with three home runs and 29 RBIs.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### Detroit Tigers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Detroit Tigers")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6f/Sean_Casey.jpg/250px-Sean_Casey.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sean_Casey.jpg)

Casey with the [Detroit Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Tigers "Detroit Tigers") in 2007

On July 31, 2006, the Pirates traded Casey to the [Detroit Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Tigers "Detroit Tigers") for minor league pitcher [Brian Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Rogers_(baseball) "Brian Rogers (baseball)").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-28) During the [2006 American League Championship Series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_American_League_Championship_Series "2006 American League Championship Series") against the [Oakland Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakland_Athletics "Oakland Athletics"), he partially tore his left calf muscle in Game 1.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-29) After coming back from his torn calf in Game 2 of the World Series, Casey became the hottest hitter for the Tigers, belting two home runs and batting .432 in five games. His .432 batting average was one of the best in Tigers' postseason history.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-30)

Casey has been active in [Big Brothers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Brothers_Big_Sisters_of_America "Big Brothers Big Sisters of America") and [Make-A-Wish Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Make-A-Wish_Foundation "Make-A-Wish Foundation"), as well as the "Casey's Crew" program, where he provided free high-priced tickets to disadvantaged youth.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-31) Casey credits his [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christians "Christians") upbringing in Pittsburgh's affluent [Upper St. Clair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_St._Clair_Township,_Pennsylvania "Upper St. Clair Township, Pennsylvania") suburb for his generosity.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-32)

After being told by [Dave Dombrowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Dombrowski "Dave Dombrowski") and [Jim Leyland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Leyland "Jim Leyland") that he would not be re-signed, Casey still praised [Mike Ilitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Ilitch "Mike Ilitch"), Dombrowski, and Jim Leyland for giving him the opportunity to come play for Detroit. Casey said "They let me know. I've had a great time with this team, the greatest year and a half of my career. It was great. But I understand the situation."[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-33)

### Boston Red Sox

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Boston Red Sox")]

On February 5, 2008, the [Boston Red Sox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Red_Sox "Boston Red Sox") announced they had signed Casey to a one-year deal.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-34) On April 9, 2008, Red Sox third baseman [Mike Lowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Lowell "Mike Lowell") injured his thumb and was then placed on the DL, first baseman [Kevin Youkilis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Youkilis "Kevin Youkilis") was moved to third, and Casey stepped in as the starting first baseman[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-35) and exploded by making some good defensive plays and hitting .318 with five RBIs in his first seven games despite missing games in [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") due to a [stiff neck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neck_stiffness "Neck stiffness") he received during the 18-hour flight.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-36) He was on the disabled list from April 26 through May 12, and returned as a significant part-time player, finishing the regular season with a .773 OPS on 199 at-bats in 69 games.

Casey was suspended by the [MLB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MLB "MLB") for three games after his actions in the [Coco Crisp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coco_Crisp "Coco Crisp")–[James Shields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Shields_(pitcher) "James Shields (pitcher)") brawl.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-37)

## Post-playing career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Post-playing career")]

Casey announced his retirement on January 25, 2009, at the age of 34, having played 12 seasons of Major League Baseball. He accepted a position as a baseball analyst for [MLB Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MLB_Network "MLB Network").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-38) He appeared on _[MLB Tonight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MLB\_Tonight "MLB Tonight")_, the Spring Training series _30 Clubs in 30 Days_, the children-focused weekly interview and demonstration show _Play Ball_ and MLB Network's special event coverage throughout the year.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:0-4)

On July 3, 2009, Casey sat in for Red Sox [color commentator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_commentator "Color commentator")[Jerry Remy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerry_Remy "Jerry Remy"), calling the first game for his old team. On January 14, 2011, the Reds announced that Casey would do [color commentary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_commentator "Color commentator") for 15 telecasts on [Fox Sports Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Sports_Ohio "Fox Sports Ohio") during the 2011 season.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-39)

The [New York Yankees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Yankees "New York Yankees") hired Casey as their [hitting coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hitting_coach "Hitting coach") on July 10, 2023.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-40)

## Awards and accomplishments

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Awards and accomplishments")]

*   [National League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_League_(baseball) "National League (baseball)")[All-Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball_All-Star_Game "Major League Baseball All-Star Game"), 1999, 2001, 2004
*   [Hutch Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hutch_Award "Hutch Award"), 1999 given to the player who personifies the spirit, courage and integrity of former manager Fred Hutchinson.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:3-22)
*   Inducted into the [University of Richmond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Richmond "University of Richmond"), Department of Athletics Hall of Fame[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:1-11) in 2003.

With [Conan O'Brien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conan_O'Brien "Conan O'Brien"), Casey is a founder of Labels Are For Jars,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-41) an innovative anti-hunger organization based in [Lawrence, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence,_Massachusetts "Lawrence, Massachusetts").

In a May 16, 2007, _[Sports Illustrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated "Sports Illustrated")_ Player's Poll,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:4-23) Casey won the distinction of being considered the "friendliest player in baseball", after winning 46% of the votes. 464 MLB players participated in the survey. [Hal McCoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hal_McCoy "Hal McCoy"), a Cincinnati Reds beat writer for 35 years, has said, "There's no debate, and there never will be a debate. Sean Casey is the nicest guy in professional baseball. Ever."

On August 26, 2008, Casey was inducted into the Irish American Baseball Hall of Fame.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-42)

On January 29, 2009, Casey was inducted into the Kinston Professional Baseball Hall of Fame.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-43)

Casey was inducted to the [Cincinnati Reds Baseball Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati_Reds_Hall_of_Fame_and_Museum "Cincinnati Reds Hall of Fame and Museum") (along with [Dan Driessen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dan_Driessen "Dan Driessen") and [John Reilly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Reilly_(baseball) "John Reilly (baseball)")) on June 23, 2012.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-:2-12)

In 2014, Casey was inducted into the [Virginia Sports Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia_Sports_Hall_of_Fame_and_Museum "Virginia Sports Hall of Fame and Museum").[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-44)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sean_Casey_(baseball)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Casey resides in Upper St. Clair Township, Pennsylvania, with his wife, Sarah. He has four children—Andrew, Jake, Carli, and Jillian—from his previous marriage to Mandi Casey.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-reflection-6)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sean_Casey_(baseball)#cite_note-r855-45)

**Casey** are a Welsh [rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_music "Rock music") band from [South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Wales "South Wales"), [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"). Formed in 2014, under the name **Well Wisher**, the band began as a studio only project by Tom Weaver and Liam Torrance, before expanding into a live performing quintet playing a style of emotional and [dynamic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamics_(music) "Dynamics (music)") music based in [hardcore punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardcore_punk "Hardcore punk"), [shoegaze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoegaze "Shoegaze") and [post-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-rock "Post-rock"). Following the release of two studio albums and two EPs, the band disbanded in 2019, however reformed at the end of 2022. Their third studio album _How to Disappear_ was released on 13 January 2024. The band's current lineup consists of Tom Weaver (vocals), Toby Evans (guitar) and Adam Smith (bass).

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Casey_(band)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### Formation, _Haze (You Buried it)_ and _Fade_ (2014–2015)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Casey_(band)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Formation, Haze (You Buried it) and Fade (2014–2015)")]

Following his departure from [Continents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continents_(band) "Continents (band)"), Tom Weaver was approached by Liam Torrance, formerly the guitarist of Hot Damn, to begin a new project. At this point, Weaver had become disheartened by touring, leading to him declining the offer until Torrance suggested the band be solely studio based, refraining from playing live. The duo then entered the studio, writing four songs, and soon rekindling their want to perform live. Because of this, they enlisted additional guitarist Toby Evans, drummer Max Nicolai and bassist Scott Edwards and took the name Well Wisher.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Burch,_2018-1) On 18 May 2014, they self-released the two track EP _Haze (You Buried It)_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Redrupt,_2018-2) Following their second live performance, Well Wisher went on a brief hiatus as Weaver auditioned for the vacant vocalist spot in [Northlane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northlane "Northlane"), at Torrence's suggestion. Once Northlane's new vocalist was instead announced as Marcus Bridge, Well Wisher's hiatus ended.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Burch,_2018-1)

On 1 December 2014, Well Wisher changed their name to Casey, under pressure from another UK band using the name Well Wisher.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Clash,_2023-3)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Burch,_2018-1) The name Casey was derived from both Weaver's love of the album _Casey_ by the Rise of Science, as well as Torrence's tribute to the late [Hawthorne Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawthorne_Heights "Hawthorne Heights") guitarist, Casey Calvert.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-4) In April 2015, the band supported Burning Down Alaska alongside [Acres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acres_(band) "Acres (band)"). Following this tour, Edwards departed from the group and was replaced by Adam Smith.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-5) On 1 May 2015, they self-released their second EP _Fade_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Punktastic_-_Love_is_Not_Enough-6) The EP gained the attention of [Hassle Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hassle_Records "Hassle Records"), who soon signed the band.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Buchanan-7) Between 17 and 23 May 2015, they toured the UK supporting [Capsize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capsize_(band) "Capsize (band)") alongside ['68](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'68_(band) "'68 (band)").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-8)

### _Love is Not Enough_ and _Where I Go When I Am Sleeping_ (2016–2019)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Casey_(band)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Love is Not Enough and Where I Go When I Am Sleeping (2016–2019)")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Casey_band.png/250px-Casey_band.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Casey_band.png)

Casey performing live in 2018

On 29 February 2016, the band's single "Darling" was premiered on [Huw Stephens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huw_Stephens "Huw Stephens")'s show on [BBC Radio 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_1 "BBC Radio 1"), being officially released alongside a music video on 6 March. This came with the announcement of the release of the four track EP _Darling_, only available on vinyl during the band's mainland Europe tour supporting Burning Down Alaska between 4 and 26 March.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-9) On 13 July, they announced the release of their debut album _Love is Not Enough_ through Hassle Records, which would also include the single "Darling".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-10) During summer 2016, the band cancelled a number of tour dates following Weaver suffering a flare up of [Bell's palsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell's_palsy "Bell's palsy").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Team_Rock_-_Casey-11) They released the album's song "Haze" as a single on 5 September[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-12) before the album was officially on 23 September 2016.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Kill_Your_Stereo-13)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Buchanan-7)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Punktastic_-_Love_is_Not_Enough-6) To support the album, the band embarked on a UK headline tour between 22 and 25 September.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-14) Between 7 and 12 November, they supported [Being as an Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Being_as_an_Ocean "Being as an Ocean") on their UK headline tour, alongside Burning Down Alaska and Capsize.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-15) On 21 August 2017, _Love is Not Enough'_ s song "Ceremony" was released as a single,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-16) and on 19 April 2017, the album's song "Little Bird" was released a single.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Kill_Your_Stereo-13)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-New_Noise_-_Little_Bird-17) Between 17 and 27 April, they toured Europe as a part of the _Impericon_ tour alongside [Thy Art is Murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thy_Art_is_Murder "Thy Art is Murder"), [Miss May I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_May_I "Miss May I") and Being as an Ocean.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-18)

On 4 December 2017, the band released the single "Fluorescents" and announced the release of their second album through [Rise Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rise_Records "Rise Records").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-19) The album was originally announced to be titled _This Routine is Hell_, a reference to the Dutch post-hardcore band of the same name, however it was soon changed to _Where I Go When I Am Sleeping_.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-20) Between 5 and 13 December, they toured the UK as a part of the _[Kerrang!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerrang! "Kerrang!")_ tour, headlined by [the Amity Affliction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Amity_Affliction "The Amity Affliction") and also featuring [Boston Manor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Manor_(band) "Boston Manor (band)") and [Vukovi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vukovi "Vukovi").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-21) The album's second single "Phosphenes" was then released on 30 January 2018,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-22) followed by "Bruise" on 27 February.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-23)_Where I Go When I Am Sleeping_ was officially released on 16 March 2018, and was supported by a UK headline tour in March and April, supported by Endless Heights and [Rarity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rarity_(band) "Rarity (band)").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-24) Between 6 and 15 July 2018, they headlined an Australian tour with support from [Stateside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stateside_(band) "Stateside (band)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Burch,_2018-1) On 1 December 2018 the band released a statement explaining that they had decided to disband following a final UK and European tour and a one-off headline show in the US in 2019.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Redrupt,_2018-2)

### Post-breakup and reformation (2020–present)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Casey_(band)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Post-breakup and reformation (2020–present)")]

In the years following Casey's disbandment, Smith formed the bands Asidhara[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-25) and Mourn, which was with members of Continents and Wilderness, and released their debut single on 5 August 2021,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-26) while Nicolai and Torrance formed Exit Dream alongside vocalist Wesley Thompson, formerly of [Napoleon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_(band) "Napoleon (band)") and [Climates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climates_(band) "Climates (band)"), and session musician Rob Hawkins.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-27) During this time, Nicolai also became the drummer for Mouth Culture[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-28) and Evans would sometimes perform as a live member for [Holding Absence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holding_Absence "Holding Absence").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-30)

On 1 December 2022, the band announced that they had reformed and that they had booked five tour date in the United Kingdom and mainland Europe between 12 and 20 January 2023.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-31) After every one of the dates sold out, they announced on 11 December that had booked additional dates in London and Oberhausen and upgraded the date in Manchester.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-32) In a January 2023 interview with _[Clash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clash\_(magazine) "Clash (magazine)")_ magazine, Weaver explained the reunion came about when Torrence contacted him about reforming only days after his split from his fiancée, which Torrence was unaware of. In the following weeks, the band's final lineup then began to meet one another, and soon began writing again.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Clash,_2023-3) On 6 December 2022, they released the single "Great Grief", the first song written as a band following their reunion,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-33) which was followed on 3 January 2023, by the single "Atone".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-34) On 15 September, they released the single "Puncture Wounds To Heaven", and announced it would be a part of the upcoming third studio album. Between 19 September and 1 October, they headlined a tour of the United States [[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-35) On 26 October, they released the single "How to Disappear", and announced the release of their studio album of the same name, which was eventually released on 12 January 2024.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-36) The album's third single was "Bite Through My Tongue" was released on 30 November.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-37) Between 26 March and 14 April 2024, they will tour the United Kingdom and mainland Europe in support of the album.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-38) The band toured North American alongside [Holding Absence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holding_Absence "Holding Absence") in January 2024. This was followed by a UK and European tour in March and April, which included several appearances at [Impericon Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impericon_Festival "Impericon Festival").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-39)

On 22 September 2025, Torrance announced his decision to leave the band to focus on his family.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-40) On 9 March 2026, Nicolai confirmed that he had also decided to leave the band towards the end of 2025.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-41) Both will rejoin the band as touring members for the _Love Is Not Enough_ 10th anniversary tour between 22 September and 4 October 2026.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-42)

### Musical style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Casey_(band)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Musical style")]

Critics have categorised Casey's music as [post-hardcore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-hardcore "Post-hardcore"),[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Bring_the_Noise_-_Love_is_Not_Enough-43)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Kill_Your_Stereo-13)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Team_Rock_-_Casey-11)[dreamcore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dreamcore_(music) "Dreamcore (music)"),[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Stewart,_2025-44)[melodic hardcore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melodic_hardcore "Melodic hardcore"),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Kill_Your_Stereo-13)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Love_is_Not_Enough-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-New_Noise_-_Love_is_Not_Enough-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Unraveled_-_Tom_Waver-47)[emo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emo "Emo")[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Punk_Rock_Theory_-_Love_is_Not_Enough-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-49) and [shoegazing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoegazing "Shoegazing").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-50) They often make use of elements of [post-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-rock "Post-rock"),[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-51)[indie rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indie_rock "Indie rock"), [post-metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-metal "Post-metal"),[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-52)[hardcore punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardcore_punk "Hardcore punk")[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Alternative_Press_-_Love_is_Not_Enough-53)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-New_Noise_-_Love_is_Not_Enough-46) and [screamo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screamo "Screamo").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-54) They were a forefront band in the 2010s dreamcore movement, which was based around the YouTube channel Dreambound, where bands merged screamo and melodic hardcore with post-rock and shoegaze.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Stewart,_2025-44) Their music is experimental and makes use of elements including ambient and spoken word parts.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Team_Rock_-_Casey-11) The band's lyrics often discuss the bleaker sides of Weaver's life and health, with _Love is not Enough_ discussing heartbreak, while _Where I Go When I Am Sleeping_ included topics such as his [bipolar disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bipolar_disorder "Bipolar disorder"), [ulcerative colitis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulcerative_colitis "Ulcerative colitis") and [osteogenesis imperfecta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteogenesis_imperfecta "Osteogenesis imperfecta"), as well as his survived heart attack, stroke and car crash.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Clash,_2023-3)

The _[BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC")_ called their music at "one moment as atmospheric as [65DaysOfStatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/65daysofstatic "65daysofstatic") or [Explosions In The Sky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explosions_In_The_Sky "Explosions In The Sky"), the next as fierce and intense as anything in [Deftones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deftones "Deftones")' back catalogue [sic]".[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-55)_Bring the Noise_ it as "packed to the rafters with emotionally charged guitar lines and captivating, heartfelt lyrics".[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Bring_the_Noise_-_Love_is_Not_Enough-43)_[Alternative Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative\_Press\_(magazine) "Alternative Press (magazine)")_ called it a "mix of rhythmic atmosphere, spoken word, hardcore guitar and more into the tracks guaranteed to move you and tell you a vivid story.",[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-Alternative_Press_-_Love_is_Not_Enough-53)

In an interview with _Music&Riots_, Weaver stated that the band try not to consider genre when writing their music, explaining "if you take 20 second snapshots throughout the record we could just as easily be [Comeback Kid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comeback_Kid_(band) "Comeback Kid (band)") as we could [Sigur Rós](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sigur_R%C3%B3s "Sigur Rós"). I think in the internet age the concept of genre is becoming less and less relevant. People are fusing soundscapes in such diverse and dramatic ways that trying to pigeonhole an artist is becoming more difficult than it's ever been. We just make music that we love, if people listen to it and it resonates with them, then the genre is of no consequence".[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casey_(band)#cite_note-65)
